name: Yuddha Kanda
title: Yuddha Kanda: The War in Lanka and Rama’s Return to Ayodhya
description: Follow Yuddha Kanda through Vibhishana’s refuge, the bridge, the war, Ravana’s death, Sita’s fire ordeal and Rama’s coronation, with chapter references.
dek: Finding Sita has made rescue possible. The next book asks what war will cost, how an enemy should be treated, and whether victory can repair everything that has been broken.
summary: Yuddha Kanda tells of the march to Lanka, Vibhishana’s refuge, the building of the bridge and the war against Ravana. After Ravana’s death it narrates Sita’s fire ordeal, the journey home, the reunion with Bharata and Rama’s coronation.
editionNote: References follow K. M. K. Murthy’s 128-sarga Yuddha Kanda at ValmikiRamayan.net. Other editions, including the Critical Edition, use different divisions. Lanka Kanda is a familiar alternative designation in some Ramayana traditions, but references here use Yuddha Kanda.

sections.heading: The news of Sita becomes a plan of action
paragraphs: Rama honours Hanuman for accomplishing what seemed almost impossible. His report gives the allies information about Lanka, its defences and Sita’s condition. Yet Rama now has to solve a problem larger than the messenger’s crossing: an army must reach the island and remain capable of fighting there.

Sugriva encourages him, and the forces march toward the ocean. On the other side, Ravana consults his ministers. Praise and assurances of strength fill the court. The contrast between useful advice and flattering speech will become one of the book’s recurring political concerns.

sections.heading: Vibhishana leaves his brother and asks for refuge
paragraphs: Vibhishana repeatedly urges Ravana to return Sita. He describes the danger of continuing in an action that has already brought disaster closer. Ravana treats the unwelcome advice as hostility, and the disagreement ends in Vibhishana’s departure.

At Rama’s camp, his arrival prompts debate. Sugriva and others consider the risk of accepting someone from the enemy’s household. Hanuman weighs his words and conduct. Rama decides to offer protection, making refuge a matter of principle as well as military advantage.

The episode does not erase the need for judgment. It stages the risk openly before Rama makes his commitment. Vibhishana subsequently contributes knowledge of Lanka and its warriors, but that usefulness is not the only reason given for receiving him.

sections.heading: The ocean and Nala’s bridge
paragraphs: Rama seeks a passage across the ocean. When waiting brings no response, anger and the threatened use of force change the encounter. The ocean’s personified deity appears and explains how a crossing can be made without simply abolishing the nature of the sea.

Nala’s skill becomes central to building the bridge. The vanara forces bring materials and carry out the work. The account combines divine encounter with organized labour; it does not make the entire crossing the result of one hero’s solitary act.

The familiar story of every stone floating because Rama’s name is written on it should not replace the bridge-building passage in this edition. Likewise, the poem’s account and modern claims about identifying or dating physical formations are different kinds of claim.

sections.heading: Scouts, deception and a final embassy
paragraphs: The allies reach Lanka and assess the opposing forces. Spies move between the camps, descriptions establish the scale of the armies, and Ravana receives warnings he does not want to accept. Malyavan also counsels a different course.

Sita is subjected to the deception of an apparent severed head of Rama. Sarama helps restore her confidence. This is part of the war even though it does not take place between armies: misinformation is used against a captive to break her resistance.

After surveying Lanka from Suvela, Rama sends Angada as an envoy. Returning Sita remains the demand. The approach to battle contains opportunities to avoid what follows, making Ravana’s continued refusal part of the explanation for the destruction.

sections.heading: The first reversals of the war
paragraphs: The fighting opens in multiple duels and assaults. Indrajit uses concealment and extraordinary weapons against Rama and Lakshmana. Their apparent defeat brings fear to the allies and anguish to Sita, who is shown the fallen brothers. Trijata offers a different reading of what she sees.

Garuda’s arrival releases the brothers from the serpent weapon’s bonds. Further commanders enter the battle, including Dhumraksha, Vajradamshtra, Akampana and Prahasta. Their deaths do not immediately end Lanka’s resistance.

Ravana himself fights. The sequence of danger, recovery and renewed combat prevents the war from becoming a simple straight line toward a predetermined victory. The allies repeatedly need rescue, information, treatment and encouragement.

sections.heading: Kumbhakarna knows the error and still fights
paragraphs: Ravana orders Kumbhakarna to be awakened. The sleeping warrior’s size and appetite make his arrival spectacular, but the conversation with his brother gives him more than a monstrous body. He can recognize the flawed decision that has brought the kingdom to this point.

Kumbhakarna nevertheless chooses to fight for Ravana. His intervention terrifies and scatters the vanaras before Rama kills him. Loyalty here does not necessarily coincide with approval of the cause being served.

Further warriors fall, including Narantaka, Trishiras and Atikaya. Ravana’s grief grows, yet loss does not lead him to release Sita. The deaths of those closest to him instead pull him further into the war.

sections.heading: Healing, illusion and the death of Indrajit
paragraphs: Another devastating attack leaves the allied forces in need of help. Hanuman’s journey for medicinal herbs answers a crisis of survival. The mountain episode belongs to Yuddha Kanda, not to the earlier search for Sita in Sundara Kanda.

Indrajit creates an illusory Sita and appears to kill her, spreading despair among those who witness it. Vibhishana explains the deception and the importance of interrupting Indrajit’s ritual preparations. Lakshmana goes with support to confront him.

The combat ends in Indrajit’s death. Lanka’s grief is not confined to Ravana; women lament their dead, and the narrative lets the cost of the war be heard from the other side. A complete account should retain these voices alongside the victories of Rama’s allies.

sections.heading: The final confrontation with Ravana
paragraphs: The final phase includes further commanders’ deaths, another grave injury to Lakshmana and another mission for healing herbs. The story should not collapse all wounds and all healing episodes into a single scene. Different crises call Hanuman into action at different points.

Rama and Ravana meet in a sustained contest. Matali serves as Rama’s charioteer. In the edition followed here, Agastya’s instruction includes the Aditya Hridaya hymn in sarga 105. Rama eventually kills Ravana in sarga 108.

Victory is followed by funeral responsibility. Rama directs that Ravana receive the rites due to the dead, while Mandodari and the other women lament. Vibhishana is installed. The defeated king’s conduct has been condemned, but his body is not left outside the obligations that death places on the living.

sections.heading: Sita’s fire ordeal must not disappear from the reunion
paragraphs: Hanuman carries news of victory to Sita. When he proposes punishing her guards, she argues against retaliation. Her response introduces restraint at the very moment when the victors possess the power to inflict it.

The meeting with Rama is then painful rather than immediately celebratory. His public words question her position after captivity. Sita protests and asks for a fire to be prepared. She enters it, and Agni returns her unharmed while affirming her fidelity.

Rama subsequently explains his conduct in terms of public recognition of her purity. Readers and traditions have debated this explanation and the ordeal itself. The narrative, Sita’s protest and Rama’s stated reason should all remain visible. A devotional reading need not pretend the scene is emotionally uncomplicated.

The gods appear, Rama’s divine identity is addressed, Dasharatha is encountered and the fallen allies receive restoration. These events bring the war toward closure without making the suffering that preceded them unreal.

sections.heading: The journey home completes Bharata’s waiting
paragraphs: Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and their companions travel in the Pushpaka. Rama points out places connected with their journey, turning the return into a recollection of what exile has cost and made possible. A landscape once crossed in uncertainty is revisited with the story now known.

Hanuman goes ahead to Bharata. His message closes the long suspense of the brother who has governed in Rama’s name. Bharata prepares the welcome and returns the responsibility he has held. The coronation restores Rama to Ayodhya after the fourteen-year exile.

Later traditions connect Rama’s victory with [Dussehra](/festivals/dussehra) and his homecoming with [Diwali](/festivals/diwali). Those festival associations deserve their own explanation; the narrative of the return is not itself a modern festival calendar.

For RudraNāda’s artistic response to the epic, listen to [Ramayana: Orchestral Journey](/music/ramayana-orchestral). For what the received seven-book text narrates after the coronation, continue to [Uttara Kanda](/ramayana/uttara-kanda).

questions.question: Who builds the bridge to Lanka?
questions.answer: Nala directs the work, with the vanara forces supplying materials and building the crossing. The episode is in sarga 22 of this edition.

questions.question: Where is the Aditya Hridaya in the Ramayana?
questions.answer: In the edition followed here, Agastya’s instruction to Rama appears in Yuddha Kanda 105. Numbering differs in other editions.

questions.question: Does the Ramayana end at the coronation?
questions.answer: Yuddha Kanda closes with the coronation and its concluding passages. The received seven-book Ramayana continues with Uttara Kanda.
